lg.l: Ten distinct Squares here seen apart,
Are join’d in one by Cutter’s art.
1 Old Democritus under a tree,

l.hi: Sits on a stone with book on knee;
About him hang there many features,
Of Cats, Dogs and such like creatures,
Of which he makes Anatomy,

lg.l: The seat of black choler to see.

l.hi: Over his head appears the sky,

lg.l: And Saturn Lord of melancholy.
2 To th’ left a landscape of Jealousy,
Presents itself unto thine eye.

l.hi: A Kingfisher, a Swan, an Hern,
Two fighting Cocks you may discern,
Two roaring Bulls each other hie,

lg.l: To assault concerning Venery.

l.hi: Symbols are these; I say no more,

lg.l: Conceive the rest by that’s afore.
3 The next of Solitariness,

l.hi: A portraiture doth well express,
By sleeping dog, cat: Buck and Doe,
Hares, Coneys in the desert go:
Bats, Owls the shady bowers over,

lg.l: In melancholy darkness hover.

l.hi: Mark well: If’t be not as’t should be,

lg.l: Blame the bad Cutter, and not me.
4 I’th’ under Column there doth stand,
Inamorato with folded hand;

l.hi: Down hangs his head, terse and polite,

lg.l: Some ditty sure he doth indite.

l.hi: His lute and books about him lie,

lg.l: As symptoms of his vanity.

l.hi: If this do not enough disclose,

lg.l: To paint him, take thyself by th’ nose.
5 Hypocondriacus leans on his arm,

l.hi: Wind in his side doth him much harm,
And troubles him full sore God knows,

lg.l: Much pain he hath and many woes.

l.hi: About him pots and glasses lie,

lg.l: Newly brought from’s Apothecary.
This Saturn’s aspects signify,
You see them portrayed in the sky.
6 Beneath them kneeling on his knee,
A Superstitious man you see:

l.hi: He fasts, prays, on his Idol fixt,
Tormented hope and fear betwixt:
For hell perhaps he takes more pain,

lg.l: Than thou dost Heaven itself to gain.

l.hi: Alas poor Soul, I pity thee,
What stars incline thee so to be?

lg.l: 7 But see the Madman rage downright
With furious looks, a ghastly sight.

l.hi: Naked in chains bound doth he lie,
And roars amain he knows not why?
Observe him; for as in a glass,

lg.l: Thine angry portraiture it was.

l.hi: His picture keep still in thy presence;

lg.l: ’Twixt him and thee, there’s no difference.
8 9 Borage and Hellebore fill two scenes,

l.hi: Sovereign plants to purge the veins
Of melancholy, and cheer the heart,
Of those black fumes which make it smart;
To clear the Brain of misty fogs,

lg.l: Which dull our senses, and Soul clogs.

l.hi: The best medicine that ere God made

lg.l: For this malady, if well assayed.
10 Now last of all to fill a place,
Presented is the Author’s face;

l.hi: And in that habit which he wears,

lg.l: His Image to the world appears.

l.hi: His mind no art can well express,

lg.l: That by his writings you may guess.

l.hi: It was not pride, nor yet vainglory,

lg.l: (Though others do it commonly)

l.hi: Made him do this: if you must know,

lg.l: The Printer would needs have it so.

l.hi: Then do not frown or scoff at it,

lg.l: Deride not, or detract a whit.

l.hi: For surely as thou dost by him,

lg.l: He will do the same again.

l.hi: Then look upon’t, behold and see,

lg.l: As thou lik’st it, so it likes thee.

l.hi: And I for it will stand in view,

lg.l: Thine to command, Reader Adieu.
